I will keep my land in the standard winter wheat and summer maize rotation. In Quzhou County, that is still the most reliable way for me to use the full year, match the local climate, and make use of machinery efficiently. At my age, I would not choose labor-intensive vegetables or highly speculative cash crops. I would rather grow crops I understand deeply, can manage on time, and can sell easily. Because my education level is high, I would pay close attention to seed choice, fertilizer balance, irrigation timing, and pest thresholds instead of farming by habit alone.

For winter wheat, I will use improved seed, keep plant population moderate, and focus on stable tillering, strong stems, and good grain filling. I will use plough tillage before sowing because I want a clean seedbed and better root development after the summer maize season. I will apply nitrogen in split doses, with part at sowing and the rest at jointing, and I will not let nitrogen get too high because that raises lodging risk. I will irrigate mainly at overwintering recovery, jointing, and grain filling if moisture is short. For pests and diseases, I will spray only when pressure justifies it, but I will assume a few applications for weeds, aphids, and common fungal disease control.

For summer maize, I will plant quickly right after wheat harvest so I do not lose heat units or soil moisture. I will use hybrid seed because yield stability matters more to me than saving seed. I will use rotary tillage or quick residue-assisted preparation so I can turn the field around fast after wheat. Fertilizer will be strong enough to support grain filling but not excessive, and I will place more emphasis on nitrogen and potassium because maize removes a lot. Irrigation will depend on rainfall, but I will plan for a few key waterings around seedling establishment, big flare, and silking if rain is poor. Pest control will be moderate and timely, mainly for borers, armyworm, and foliar disease if they appear. Overall, I will choose a conservative, high-probability plan: fewer surprises, full use of the land, and stable grain output.
